full_judgment:
Mr. Md. Tafazzul Islam, J: Both the appeals i.e. First Appeal No. 193 and. 194 of 1999 are directed against the judgment and decree dated 6.4.99 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge. Additional Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 13 of 1994 and Title Suit No. 22 of 1993 by which both the suits were decreed in favour of the plaintiffs. 

2. Mr. Abdul Gani and Abdul Latif, who are the plaintiff-respondents in both the appeals, tiled Title Suit No. 26 of 1990, which on transfer was renumbered as Title Suit No. 22 of 1993, praying for declaration amongst others, that they are owners of 8 annas 4 gondas I kara and 2 kranties of land, which is equivalent to 62 decimals of land. In the plaint it was stated inter-alia that Abdul Hakim and Saijuddin, two brothers, were the owners of 11.61 acres of land in Khatian No. 29 which contained C.S. Plot No. 44 and then by amicable partition late Abdul Hakim, amongst others, got 1.21 acres of land in C.S. Plot No. 44, i.e. the suit plot, and after Abdul Hakim died. Halimon Bibi his 3rd wife, Rahatun Bibi, Suratun Nessa daughters through his first wife, Ismail and Nurbanu, his sons and daughter through his second wife and the plaintiffs, who are his sons through the above Halimon, his third wife, became owners of the suit land and that there had been no partition of the suit land amongst the heirs of Abdul Hakim either by amicable settlement or through Court. Then Halimun died leaving her 2 annas share in the suit land and thus each of the plaintiff got one anna share while the above heirs of Abdul Hakim were possessing the suit land in ejmali, the government acquired the same in L.A. Case No. 2 of 1987-88 and the defendant No. 4, who is entrusted with the duty of praying the amount of compensation against the above acquisition, after verifying the papers prepared the award in the names of the plaintiffs against acquisition of .62 acres of land out of 1.21 acres of land as contained in C.S. Plot No. 44 and issued notice dated 24.12.89 upon them under Section 7(3) of Ordinance, 1982 and after receiving the aforesaid notice, the plaintiffs went to the office of the defendant No. 4 but came to know that the defendant No. 1 lodged claim for compensation for the entire 1.21 acres of land of C.S. Plot No. 44 and then the plaintiff requested the defendant No. 4 for initiating a miscellaneous case to ascertain the shares of the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1 in the amount of compensation payable against acquisition but the defendant No. 4 did not initiate the miscellaneous case and the defendant No. 1 is trying to withdraw the entire compensation money and if the defendant No. 1 succeeded in withdrawing the entire compensation amount, the plaintiff would suffer irreparable loss and injury. 

3. The aforesaid Abdul Gani and Abdul Latif also filed Title Suit No. 241 of 1994, which on transfer was renumbered as T.S. No. 13 of 1994, '--tying for declaration that both the sale Deed Nos. 4512 and 4513 dated 8.12..; are fraudulent, collusive and not binding upon them. 

4. The appellants, who are the defendants in the above Title Suit No. 22 of 1993 contested the suit and filed written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint and stating inter alia that the suit is not maintainable as no consequential relief was sought and the suit is also barred by limitation and further the defendants also acquired title in the suit land by adverse possession and they also contested. Title Suit No. 13 of 1994 and filed written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint and stating inter alia that the heirs of Abdul Hakim by Sale Deed No. 4512 dated 8.12.45 out of 1.21 acres of land, sold .62 acres of land to Zafar Ali, the father of defendant Nos. 1-3, and by sale deed No. 4513 executed on them the same day also sold the balance .59 acres of land in to Babar Ali, son of Wahed Ali, and thereby the right of title and interest of the heirs of late Abdul Hakim in the entire suit extinguished and subsequently by sale deed dated 9.12.47 Babor Ali sold the above .59 acres of land to Zafar Ali and thus Zafar All possessed 1.21 acres of land on the basis of the said sale deeds and also adversely and thereafter during S.A. operation the name of Zafar All was duly recorded in the S.A. Khatian. 

5. Both the plaintiffs and the defendants examined 4 witnesses from each side and also filed documents and the learned Sub-ordinate Judge after hearing both the suits analogously, decreed both the suits holding that apart from others. Ext. 2 also proved the possession of the plaintiff in the suit land and that the suits are not barred by limitation. 

6. Mr. Md. Khalilur Rahman the learned Advocate for the defendant appellants in both the appeals submits that Ismail, was not at all entitled to sell the share of his step brothers, the minor plaintiffs, without permission of the competent court and so the Sale deed Nos. 4512 and 4513 both dated 8.12.45 so far those relates to the shares of the minors are void but however since the defendants on the basis of an invalid transfer had been in adverse possession of the entire 1.21 acres of land since 1945, they acquired title, over the land belonging to the minor plaintiffs as well as the land belonging to Halimunnessa and so the title of the plaintiffs, as well as Halimunnessa, if any, had been extinguished by the adverse possession. Mr. Rahman further submits that in the writ-ten statement the defendants took specific plea of adverse possession and the wit-nesses of the plaintiff failed to prove their possession in the suit land and further the plaintiff did not produce any evidence, even a rent receipt, to show that for this long 45 years the plaintiff ever paid any rent for the suit land whereas the D.Ws. proved the possession of the defendant Nos. 1 and 3 in the suit land and further the S.A. and R.S. records also show the open and adverse possession of defendants in the suit land and the plaintiff also did not take any step for correction of the aforesaid S.A. as well as R.S. record of right and further, in the plaint the plain-tiffs stated that they are in ejmali possession of the suit land without at all stating that they are possessing the northern side and in the plaint there is also nothing regarding mode of possession i.e. by cultivating themselves or cultivating through borgadars and further in the plaint the boundaries of the suit land were also not given and so evidence led in respect of the matters not mentioned in the plaint should not be taken into consideration at all as being beyond pleading. Mr. Rahman lastly submits that in the present case transfer has been made not within relations but to strangers and so the principle laid down in 39 DLR(AD)-22 will not be applicable and further the plaintiffs, not being in possession of the suit land. were required to seek consequential relief by way of restraining the defendants from withdrawing the compensation money or any other way and the plaintiffs having not done so, the suit must fail. 

7. Mr. Mahabuby Alam, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondent Nos. 1 and 2 in both the appeals, submits that the plaintiffs were neither required to state in the plaint that they were possess-ing northern portion of the suit land nor state in the plaint the mode of possession i.e. cultivating the suit land themselves or through borgagars and further, the plain-tiff was also not required to describe in the plaint the boundaries of the suit land as the same was clearly identifiable and that the statement made in the plaint to the effect that the plaintiffs possessed the suit land in ejmali was enough for seeking the declaration that they are the owners of .62 acres of land in view of the principle laid down in the case of Hazera Begum Vs. Rewshanara Begum 39 DLR AD 22 and the failure of the plaintiff to file a rent receipt in support of their possession will not defeat their claim of possession and that for claiming the amount of compensation, which is lying with the defendant No. 4, a third party, no consequential relief is required to be sought. Further the defendants, in their pleading, did not specifically plead that they and also their predecessors acquired title by adverse possession and if even for arguments sake it is assumed that plea of adverse possession has been specifically taken, the onus was upon the defendants to prove acquisition of title by adverse possession which they failed Mr. Alam lastly submits that since in Title Suit No. 13 of 1994 the plaintiff sought relief to the effect that Sale Deed Nos. 4512 and 4513 dated 8.12.45 are not binding upon them, it will be deemed that the plaintiffs are still co-sharers of the suit and further Halima, being admittedly alive till 1985, her share to the extent of 2 annas in 1.21 acres could not be extinguished by the above Sale Deeds dated 8.12.45 and she also can claim to be co-sharer in respect of her 2 annas share. 

8. Heard the learned Advocates. 

9. Since Mr. Rahman admitted that sale deed Nos. 4512 and 4513 dated 8.12.45, so far those relates to transfer of shares of the minors, are void and so the sole question if whether the defendants were strangers and they, on the basis of the sale deeds possessed the suit land openly and adversely against the title of the plaintiffs and thereby acquired title by way of adverse possession against minors and also Halimunnessa who had 2 annas share in the suit land. 

10. In the plaint the plaintiff merely stated that he possessed the suit land in ejmali and there is no adverment in the plaint to the effect that the plaintiff possessed the suit land on its northern portion. However, P.W. 1 in his deposition stated that the plaintiff possessed the northern side of its suit land. Regarding mode of possession there is nothing in the plaint and P.W. 1 also did not say regarding mode of possession but P.W. 2 in his examination in Chief stated that for 5/7 years by cultivated the suit land on borga but in cross stated that Gani Mia and others themselves used to cultivate the suit land and they had commonness. P.W. 3 stated that the plaintiff used to cultivate Khama Paddy in the suit land. P.W. 4, in his examination in Chief, stated that the plaintiffs cultivated about 2 pakhis of land in northern side of the suit land but in cross he stated that the plaintiff cultivated the land on borga. 

11. On the other hand, D.W. 1 the Manager of the defendant who deposed in support the case of the defendant, has his knowledge only from 197.6 when he joined as manager and so his evidence regarding possession is of no importance being hearsay. D.W. 2 who owns land adjacent to the suit land stated that he saw that the sons of Zafar Ali possessed the suit land and they sold the suit land to the defendant No. 1 and that defendant No. 1 possessed the suit land for about 10 years and at the time of acquisition, the defendant No. 1 was in possession of the suit land and he never saw the plaintiffs possessing the suit land. The plaintiff could not get much in cross examining D.W. 2, D.W. 3, who owned land to the western side of the suit land stated that Zafar All and Babor Ali possessed the suit land and Babor Ali sold his land to Zafar Ali and that the heirs of Zafar Ali possessed the suit land for about 50 years and the heirs of Jafar Ali themselves used to cultivate the suit land and D.W. 3 cultivated the suit land for 8/10 years as borgader at the time of the defendant No. 1 and during his borga the plaintiff did not raise any obstruction. However at the end of his cross though it was stated. নাঃ দাগের ৬২ ১/৪ ডিং ভূমি সব সময় বাদীর ভোগ দখল করে খাইত। ইহা সত্য নহে যে, আমি বর্গা চাষ করে খাওয়ার কথা মিথ্যা বলেছি, ইহা সত্য নহে যে, আমি কথনো বর্গা চাষ করি নাই।” 

12. D.W. 4, who is the grand son of Zafar Ali, stated that his father Fazar Ali and uncle Monsur All and Moksed Ali possessed the suit land and thereafter they sold the suit land to the defendant No. 1 but in cross he stated that he was not born when Zafar Ali purchased the suit land. His age being 47 years on 16.3.99 i.e. at the time of deposition on 16.3.99 and so he appears to have been born in the year 1952 and so his deposition regarding possession of his father and uncle and also of defendant No. 1 in the suit land is valueless. 

13. Ext. 1 is the Parcha of C.S. Khatian No. 29 and Ext. 2 is the notice dated 24.12.89 under Section 7(3) of Ordinance 1982 asking the plaintiff to receive the compensation amount of Tk. 9,06,072.90 from the defendant No. 4. On the other hand the defendant in para 17(ka) of the written statement stated that by sale deed No. 4512 dated 8.12.45 the sons and daughters of Late Abdul Hakim sold .62 acres of land to Zafar Ali and they by Sale Deed No. 4513 dated 8.12.45 also sold .59 acres of land to Babar Ali and then by Sale Deed dated 9.12.74 Babar All sold said .59 acres of land to Zafar Ali and thus Zafar Ali became owner in possession of the entire 1.21 acres of land and in the aforesaid paragraph it was also stated that “এই ভাবে জাফর আলী নালিশী সি এস ৪৪ দাগের ১.২০ শতাংশ ভূমির মালিক দথলকারী সত্বাধিকারী এবং অন্যের বিরুদ্ধে দখল জনিত স্বত্বে ভোগ দখল করিতে রহেন ও থাকেন।”  So the submission of Mr. Alam that the defendants, in their pleading did not specifically pleaded acquiring of title by adverse possession are not correct. 

14. It also appears that Ext. 2 was issued on 24.12.89 whereas earlier similar notice dated 26.11.89. Ext. Cha(2), was issued in favour of the predecessors of the defendants. The notice issued under Sections 3 and 4 of the Ordinance 1982 and the award made in L.A. Case No. 2 of 1987-88 are not in the records of the pre-sent case. As It appears from the contents of both Exts. 2 and Cha (2) issued under Section 7(3) of Ordinance 1982, the names of the Surveyor and the Kanago, who initiated the above notices, are same. But Ext. Cha (2) was signed by the Additional Land Acquisition Officer on 26.11.89: i.e. about one month ago and C.S. Plot No. 44 having only 1.21. acres of land, after issuance of Ext. Cha(2) there is no scope of issuing Ext. 2 and so the contention of the appellant that Ext. 2 has been prepared subsequently cannot in the facts and circumstances of the present case, be totally ruled out because the Surveyer and the Kanango, who initiated Ext. Cha(2) asked the predecessor of the defendants to receive Tk. 17,61.201.93 against compensation of 1.21 acres of land contained in C.S. Plot No. 44 and so in the normal course of dealing, there is no scope for initiating Ext. 2 on the same date i.e. 25.11.89 in respect of part of the above 1.21 acres of land. In any view of the matter after signing of Ext. Cha(2). Ext. 2 though shown to be initiated on the same date became value-less because the acquisition authority was not of all competent to give compensation for acquisition of more than 1.21 acres of land. So in the facts and circumstance of the present case, Ext. 2 does not in any way prove the possession of the plaintiff in the suit land. Further in paragraph 9 of the plaint it has been stated that the plaintiff requested the defendant No. 4 to initiate a miscellaneous case to ascertain as to who are entitled to receive compensation in what proportion and that the said miscellaneous case was not initiated by the defendant No. 4 but on the face of Ext. Cha(2) it will be deemed that there was already an award in the names of Zafar Ali and another and in the aforesaid circumstances it was the responsibility of the plaintiff to file miscellaneous case because Ordinance 1982 does not require the Land Acquisition Officer to initiate such miscellaneous case on the request of the parties. 

15. In support of their claim of acquisition of title in the suit land by adverse possession, the defendants filed Ext. Ka, the C.S. Khatian No. 29 Ext.- Ka & Kha(1)2 Sale Deeds dated 8.12.45. Ext. Ga the Sale Deed dated 9.12.47. Ext Gha-Gha(2) i.e. the S.A. Khatians, Ext. Uma and Uma(1)2 Sale Deeds dated 18.3.78. Ext. Cha(2) notice dated 26.11.89 issued upon the predecessor of defendants under Section 7(3) of Ordinance 1982. Ext. Cha and Cha(1) are the Deeds of Indemnity by which the heirs of Abdul Hakim undertook to compensate Zafar All in case of any claim lodged by the minors, whose proper-ties were also sold by the aforesaid Deeds. Out of those, Exts. Gha, Gha(1) and Gha(2) S.A. Khatians shows that the name of Zafar Ali was recorded in the S.A. Khatian No. 49 formerly C.S. Khatian No. 29/1 and the names of Rajab Ali and Mansur Ali, who are son of Zafar Ali, were printed in R.S. Dag No. 402 and 414 which contained .62 and .59 of acres of land respectively, total of which 1.21 acres of land, and that defendant No. 1 got his name mutately in the suit land by Mutation Case No. 6453 dated 31.3.79. 

16. The case of the defendant is that though Ext. Kha and Kha(1) did not confer upon Zafar Ali and Babor Ali the title of the land held by the minors, but Exts. Kha and Kha(1) can be considered to prove possession of Zafar Ali and Babor All on the land of the plaintiffs in the year 1945 and further the defendants, being stranger to the family of late Abdul Hakim, limitation will run from the date of the transfer for the purpose of determining the claim of title of the defendants by way of adverse possession. 

17. In the case of Ezar Box Vs. r. 21 DI,R (SC) 444 cited by Mr. Rahman in sup-port of the above proposition, the brother sold certain property to a stranger claiming that he owned the property whereas the property actually belonged to him as well as his two minor brothers. The purchaser remained in possession of the suit property openly, exclusively and in assertion of his own title, mutated his name and paid rent. The minors took no step to assert their title thereto for long 21 years even after they became major. Then the minors, filed suit for asserting their right to the said property claiming that the purchaser was in possession in the suit land as co-sharer in view of purchase from their brother, a co-sharer, and as such, the plaintiffs are entitled to recover their share from the purchaser and that the question of limitation just as between the co-sharers did not arise so as to defeat their right to the property on the ground for adverse possession of the purchaser for more than 12 years. The above assertion of the minors was accepted by the trial Court as well as the appellate Court but on appeal the decision was reversed by the High Court. The Supreme Court affirmed the decision of the High Court holding that when the parties are co-sharer the possession of one of them is regarded in law as possession on behalf of them but this does not mean that a co-sharer can never possess adversely to the other co-sharer and acquire title by way of adverse possession, but however, to enable one of the co-sharer to acquire title by adverse possession as against the other co-sharer, his possession must be of such an actual, open notorious, exclusive and hostile character so as to amount to a ouster or exclusion of other co-sharer. In the aforesaid decision it was further held that it is not necessary that the adverse character of the possession should be actually brought home to the knowledge of the true owner and it is sufficient that the possession was over and without any attempt of concealment so that the person, against whom time is running out, by exercising due diligence could be aware of what is happening and that the question whether or not exclusive possession by a co-sharer amount to ouster or exclusion of other co-sharer depends upon the facts arid circumstances of each case. 

18. Further, the facts of 39 DLR (AD) 22 referred by Mr. Alam are different from the present case in as much as in the reported case the co-sharers were relations and so the possession of one co-sharers was not held adverse to the possession of the plaintiff and it was held that if transfer is made within relation or co-sharer limitation will not run from the date of transfer but if transfer is made to stranger to the family, limitation may run from the date of transfer provided there is evidence of open and adverse possession. In the present case transfer was not made to relation or co-sharer. 

19. In the case of Abdus Sattar Vs. Abdur Rahman, 44 DLR 100 cited Mr. Rahman the plaintiff filed suit for recovery of possession taking the stand that the defendants by Ext. A paid rent to Shebiat i.e. the predecessor of the plaintiffs, for the years 1362-67 B.S. and the defendants who claimed title by way of adverse possession, took the stand that they paid rent under duress. The trial Court found that the rent receipt in question was not issued under the normal circumstances and there is some foul play over it. It was held that whether the rent receipt was paid due to duress or not make no difference to decide to the question of adverse possession because the possession of the defendants became adverse in long before the alleged date of payment of rent and there cannot be any valid argument against the defendants on the basis of Ext. A. The trial court as well as High Court disbelieved the plaintiffs case for possession and dispossession but found their title in the suit land. The Appellate Division held that in such case the plain-tiffs can get recovery of possession only if the title is not lost by adverse possession pleaded by the defendants and the suit will be decided on the basis as to when the possession of the defendants became adverse to the plaintiffs and further, for adverse possession, the possession required must be adequate in continuity, in publicity and extent to show that possession was adverse to the competitor and it is not necessary that adverse possession should have been brought to the knowledge of the competitor and that it is sufficient that the possession is overt and without any attempt of concealment so that the person against whom time is running out can in exercise of due diligence may be a ware as to what happening. 

20. In the case of Shah Alam. Vs. Masuma Khatun 45 DLR (AD) 541 cited by Mr. Rahman it was contended that even if the plaintiffs are found to be in sole possession of the suit plot that will not amount to ouster of the co-sharer defendants however long the possession of the plaintiffs might be and the title of the defendants will not be extinguished in the suit plot by such possession of the plain-tiffs and as such the court below was wholly wrong in declaring the title of the plaintiffs in the entire suit plot. It was held by the Appellate Division that defendant No. 7 Khadem Ali, being a descendant of the original owner and his son also similarly being transferees from descendant of the original owner sole possession of Khadem Ali in the suit land could not have extinguished the title of his co-sharer son. But the plaintiff, being stranger to the family and having purchased from Azizur Rahman, transferee of Khadem Ali and having got exclusive possession of the suit land to the knowledge of the defendants and having mutated and recorded their names in assertion of their title and denying the title of the sons of Khadem All and paid rent from the time of their purchase continuously in spite of objection by the son of Khadem Ali, their open possession is a notorious fact and nothing but ouster of the son of Khadem All from the suit plot. 

21. It thus appears that When a co-sharer is sole possession transfers the land in his possession to a stranger to the family and such purchaser possessed the land in assertion of his title to the exclusion of other co-sharer openly, notoriously and continuously and denied the title of other co-sharers by mutating and recording his name in the record of right and paying rent separately, the same will amount to ouster of such co-sharers and such possession more than 12 years will extinguish of title of a co-sharer by way adverse possession. In the present case the S.A. and R.S. records having been pre-pared in the name of Zafar Ali and there-after in the names of Fazar Ali and Monsur Ali and subsequently Shamsuzzaman i.e. the defendant No. 1 prove that the defendant No. 1 and his predecessor in interest, possessed the suit land openly, notoriously and continuously denying title of the plaintiff. 

22. Regarding 2 annas share of Halima Bibi we are of the view that Halima Bibi, even after execution Ext. Kha and Kha(1) in the year 1945, had her 2 annas share in the suit land but due adverse possession her title in respect of 2 annas share in the suit land has also been extinguished. 

23. Since we have held that the right title and interest of the plaintiffs in respect of .62 acres of land of C.S. Plot No. 44 has been extinguished due to the adverse possession of the defendant No. 1 and his predecessor in interest and since the plaintiffs had no right title and interest in respect of .62 acres of land at the time of filing of Title Suit No. 13 of 1994, the prayer as made out in the plaint of the aforesaid suit to the effect that the sale deed No. 4512 and 4513 are illegal, fraudulent and collusive and that the plaintiff are not bound by the same, is not maintainable under Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, and accordingly the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 13 of 1994 is liable to be set aside. 

24. In the result both the appeals i.e. First Appeal No. 193 as well as 194 of 1999 are allowed without any order as to cost and the judgment and decree dated 6.4.99 passed by the learned Sub-ordinance Judge, Additional Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 13 of 1994 as well as in Title Suit No. 22 of 1993 respectively are set aside.

End.
